Expect up to 75% of total cost on a spec building versus up to 80% once space is pre-leased. Lenders substitute market evidence for a signed lease, so a current absorption study, comparable rents, and a credible lease-up budget carry the file.

industrial-construction-loans.q: What rates do industrial construction loans carry?
industrial-construction-loans.a: Pricing generally runs 6.50% to 11.00%. Banks and life insurance companies compete hardest on pre-leased build-to-suit projects backed by a credit tenant lease. Debt funds and private lenders own the speculative and heavier-lift end of the market, quoting wider spreads in exchange for higher proceeds, looser covenants, and faster execution.

industrial-construction-loans.q: What do lenders underwrite on a warehouse development, and how long does it take?
industrial-construction-loans.a: Underwriting turns on four things: the sponsor's completed industrial projects, a fixed-price or guaranteed maximum price contract with a qualified general contractor, verified market absorption, and an exit cap rate that supports a CMBS, life company, or bank takeout. Plan on 45 to 90 days from application, longer where entitlements, utilities, or environmental work are unresolved.

industrial-construction-loans.q: Is cold storage construction financed differently from dry warehouse?
industrial-construction-loans.a: Cold storage underwrites as a hybrid of real estate and equipment. Refrigeration systems, insulated panels, and slab design push costs far above dry warehouse per square foot, and lenders discount those specialized improvements when sizing against stabilized value. Expect lower loan-to-cost, a longer lease-up assumption, and pressure to identify an end user before breaking ground.

self-storage-financing.a: Self-storage financing funds the acquisition, refinance, ground-up construction, and conversion of storage facilities, including climate-controlled, multi-story urban infill, and boat and RV storage. Loan amounts run from $2 million to $30 million and above. Capital comes from CMBS conduits, life insurance companies, banks, and debt funds, all of which maintain dedicated storage appetite.

self-storage-financing.q: What rates and terms apply to a self-storage loan?
self-storage-financing.a: Self-storage rates generally run 5.50% to 9.00% with terms of 5 to 25 years. Stabilized Class A facilities in dense suburban trade areas price at the low end through life insurance companies and CMBS conduits. Transitional or lease-up facilities land at the high end, usually in a bridge-to-perm structure that refinances once occupancy stabilizes.

self-storage-financing.q: How much can I borrow against a self-storage facility?
self-storage-financing.a: Leverage reaches 75% of value on a stabilized facility with a documented operating history. Non-recourse is available from CMBS conduits and life insurance companies, while bank and construction debt usually carries a guarantee. On a lease-up facility, a bridge lender will size an initial advance on in-place income and hold back the balance until occupancy targets are met.

self-storage-financing.q: How do lenders underwrite a self-storage property?
self-storage-financing.a: Storage leases are month to month, so underwriting leans on trailing twelve month performance rather than a rent roll. Lenders compare physical occupancy against economic occupancy, test in-place rents against published street rates, review concession and rate-increase policy, and measure competing square feet per capita in the three mile trade area. Nearby new supply is the fastest way to lose proceeds.

self-storage-financing.q: How long does it take to close a self-storage loan?
self-storage-financing.a: Permanent financing through a life insurance company, bank, or CMBS conduit typically closes in 45 to 90 days, with appraisal, environmental work, and legal review setting the pace. Bridge debt on a lease-up facility or a conversion can fund in three to five weeks. Ground-up construction requests take longest because plans, budget, and contractor review are underwritten alongside the site.

hotel-motel-financing.q: What does hotel and motel financing cover?
hotel-motel-financing.a: Hotel and motel financing covers acquisition, renovation, refinance, and ground-up construction for full-service, select-service, extended-stay, boutique, and budget properties. Loan amounts run from $2 million to $50 million and above. Because hospitality income resets nightly, most of the capital comes from CMBS conduits, debt funds, and hospitality-focused bridge lenders rather than conventional banks.

hotel-motel-financing.q: What are current hotel loan rates and terms?
hotel-motel-financing.a: Hospitality pricing generally runs 6.00% to 12.00%, the widest spread of any commercial asset class. Permanent debt carries 5 to 25 year terms, fixed or floating, and prices at the low end for flag-affiliated select-service assets with steady trailing performance. Bridge and renovation debt runs 12 to 36 months and prices toward the top of that band.

hotel-motel-financing.q: What leverage is available on a hotel loan?
hotel-motel-financing.a: Leverage tops out near 70% of value, lower than most commercial property types, because a hotel re-leases every room every night and has no contractual rent to underwrite. Proceeds are usually constrained further by debt service coverage and debt yield tests applied to trailing income. Non-recourse is available through CMBS conduits.

hotel-motel-financing.q: How do lenders underwrite a hotel or motel?
hotel-motel-financing.a: Underwriters work from trailing twelve month RevPAR, average daily rate, and occupancy, then benchmark the property against its competitive set to see whether it is gaining or losing share. Remaining franchise term, brand quality scores, the reserve for furniture, fixtures, and equipment, and any pending property improvement plan all shape proceeds. An unfunded improvement plan is the most common deal killer.

hotel-motel-financing.q: How long does hotel financing take to close?
hotel-motel-financing.a: Hospitality bridge and renovation debt typically funds in three to six weeks. CMBS and other permanent hotel loans run 45 to 90 days because franchise comfort letters, brand approvals, and third-party reports sit on the critical path. Commercial Lending Solutions arranges this financing and tracks which hospitality desks hold open appetite by flag and market.

student-housing-loans.q: What counts as student housing for financing purposes?
student-housing-loans.a: Lenders treat purpose-built student housing, off-campus apartment communities with heavy student concentration, and mixed-use buildings in campus districts as student housing. Loan amounts run from $2 million to $50 million and above, funded by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac programs, CMBS conduits, banks, life insurance companies, and debt funds with dedicated student housing platforms.

student-housing-loans.q: What rates and terms are available on student housing loans?
student-housing-loans.a: Student housing pricing generally runs 5.75% to 9.50% over terms of 5 to 25 years. Agency permanent debt on a stabilized purpose-built community near a large university prices at the low end. Bridge-to-agency structures for acquisitions that need renovation or a full lease-up season price higher and carry a defined path to permanent takeout.

student-housing-loans.q: How much leverage can I get on a student housing property?
student-housing-loans.a: Leverage reaches 80% of value through agency programs, higher than most commercial asset classes, because by-the-bed leases with parental guarantors reduce credit risk. Non-recourse is standard on agency and CMBS executions. Properties beyond a comfortable walk or shuttle ride from campus are usually sized lower regardless of current occupancy.

student-housing-loans.q: How do lenders underwrite student housing?
student-housing-loans.a: The first test is the university itself: total enrollment, the multi-year enrollment trend, and whether it is a flagship or research institution. Next comes distance to campus, unit and bed configuration, and the amenity package measured against competing communities. Underwriters then review pre-leasing velocity for the coming academic year, since one missed leasing season resets income for twelve months.

student-housing-loans.q: How long does a student housing loan take to close?
student-housing-loans.a: Agency and CMBS permanent loans generally close in 45 to 90 days, while bridge debt funds faster, in three to six weeks. Timing matters more here than in other asset classes because the entire rent roll turns over at once and lenders want the coming year's pre-leasing report. Commercial Lending Solutions places these loans through agency-approved lenders.

senior-housing-financing.q: What is senior housing financing and what property types does it cover?
senior-housing-financing.a: Senior housing financing funds acquisition, construction, and refinancing of independent living, assisted living, memory care, and continuing care retirement communities. Loans run $2 million to $75 million and above. Unlike conventional real estate lending, underwriting weighs operating performance (labor, census, regulatory compliance) alongside real estate value, so lenders with healthcare expertise dominate the space.

senior-housing-financing.q: What rates and leverage are available for senior housing loans?
senior-housing-financing.a: Rates generally run 5.75% to 10.00%, with terms of 5 to 35 years and leverage up to 75% LTV. HUD 232 anchors the low end with 35-year fully amortizing non-recourse debt. Agency and CMBS execution prices in the middle. Debt funds financing census turnarounds sit at the top. A minimum debt service coverage test usually caps proceeds before LTV does.

senior-housing-financing.q: What do lenders look for in a senior housing operator?
senior-housing-financing.a: Operator quality drives the credit decision. Lenders want a management company with a multi-property track record in the same care level, clean state survey history, stable census and staffing, and audited or reviewed operating statements. Owner-operators without that depth are often required to bring in a third-party manager as a condition of closing.

senior-housing-financing.q: How long does it take to close senior housing financing?
senior-housing-financing.a: Timing varies widely by capital source. A debt fund bridge loan on an acquisition or lease-up can close in 30 to 45 days. Agency and CMBS permanent debt runs 60 to 90 days. HUD 232 delivers the best long-term terms but requires 6 to 9 months, including operator review, state survey history, and third-party reports.

senior-housing-financing.q: How does payor mix affect senior housing financing?
senior-housing-financing.a: Payor mix is the sharpest dividing line in this asset class. Private-pay independent living and assisted living attract conventional real estate lenders and the best pricing. Communities with heavy Medicaid or skilled nursing exposure carry reimbursement risk and route to healthcare-specialty lenders or HUD 232, which underwrite operations far more deeply and take longer to close.

medical-office-financing.a: Medical office financing covers acquisition, construction, and refinancing of medical office buildings, ambulatory surgery centers, urgent care facilities, and outpatient campuses, starting at $2 million. Lenders treat medical office as a defensive asset class because healthcare demand is non-discretionary and tenant buildouts are expensive to replicate, which keeps renewal rates high and vacancy low relative to conventional office.

medical-office-financing.q: What rates, terms, and leverage apply to medical office loans?
medical-office-financing.a: Medical office loans price from 5.25% to 8.50%, with terms of 5 to 25 years and leverage up to 75% LTV. Life insurance companies quote the tightest rates on stabilized, well-tenanted buildings at moderate leverage, and CMBS conduits reach the highest proceeds. Physician groups buying their own building can access long-term fixed-rate SBA 504 structures instead.

medical-office-financing.q: How do lenders underwrite medical office tenants?
medical-office-financing.a: Underwriting centers on the rent roll: tenant credit (health system versus independent physician practice), weighted average remaining lease term, and whether leases extend beyond loan maturity. Lenders also review hospital affiliation and referral patterns. Multi-tenant buildings with staggered expirations and funded tenant improvement reserves underwrite far better than a building facing near-term rollover.

medical-office-financing.q: How long does it take to close a medical office loan?
medical-office-financing.a: Bank and debt fund executions typically close in 45 to 60 days. Life insurance company and CMBS loans usually run 60 to 90 days, driven by appraisal, environmental and property condition reports, and lease review. Owner-occupied SBA 504 transactions take longer, generally 60 to 120 days, because of the second-position debenture funding process.

medical-office-financing.q: Does an on-campus location change medical office financing terms?
medical-office-financing.a: Yes. Buildings on or adjacent to a hospital campus command the best pricing and leverage because the hospital relationship supports tenant retention. Off-campus multi-tenant and single-tenant medical office is broadly lendable but priced wider. The common trap is a ground lease under an on-campus building: lenders require the ground lease term to extend well beyond loan maturity.

sale-leaseback-financing.q: What is a commercial real estate sale-leaseback?
sale-leaseback-financing.a: In a sale-leaseback, a business sells the real estate it occupies to an investor and simultaneously signs a long-term net lease to stay in the building. The seller keeps full operational use of the facility and converts trapped equity into cash. The buyer acquires a net-leased asset backed by the operating company's lease and corporate guarantee.

sale-leaseback-financing.q: How much capital does a sale-leaseback unlock compared with a mortgage?
sale-leaseback-financing.a: A sale-leaseback monetizes essentially 100% of the property's value, while a mortgage on the same asset typically advances 65% to 75% of value. The tradeoff is that the business gives up ownership and future appreciation, and takes on a long-term rent obligation in place of amortizing debt service.

sale-leaseback-financing.q: What financing terms apply to the investor buying the property?
sale-leaseback-financing.a: NNN acquisition debt on sale-leaseback assets prices from 5.25% to 7.50%, with terms of 10 to 25 years and leverage up to 75% LTV. Life insurance companies and CMBS conduits are the deepest capital sources, non-recourse is available at institutional size, and closings generally run 45 to 90 days from application.

sale-leaseback-financing.q: How do lenders underwrite the lease and the seller's credit?
sale-leaseback-financing.a: Lenders test three things: remaining lease term relative to loan maturity, the financial strength of the operating company guaranteeing the lease, and rent coverage measured against the tenant's earnings at that location. Investment-grade or audited private guarantors with 15 or more years of remaining lease term draw the best pricing and the highest proceeds.

sale-leaseback-financing.q: What is the most common mistake in structuring a sale-leaseback?
sale-leaseback-financing.a: Setting rent above market. A seller can raise the sale price by agreeing to inflated rent, but appraisers and lenders underwrite to market rent, so the buyer's financing shrinks and the deal reprices or dies at the closing table. Rent set at a defensible market level, with modest annual escalations, keeps the transaction financeable. Commercial Lending Solutions arranges both sides of these transactions.

cpace-financing.a: C-PACE stands for Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy. It is long-term fixed-rate capital for energy efficiency, renewable energy, resiliency, and related building improvements, repaid as a special assessment on the property tax bill rather than as a conventional mortgage. Programs are authorized state by state and are available in 38 or more states plus the District of Columbia.

cpace-financing.q: What are C-PACE rates and terms?
cpace-financing.a: C-PACE pricing runs 6.50% to 8.50% fixed, with amortization matched to the useful life of the improvements, generally 10 to 30 years. Project sizes start at $2 million and run past $30 million. The assessment is non-recourse, requires no personal guarantee, and transfers to the next owner automatically when the property sells.

Eligible measures typically include HVAC replacement, roofing and insulation, LED lighting, windows, solar and battery storage, EV charging infrastructure, water conservation systems, and in many states seismic and fire code retrofits. Eligibility is set by the individual state or county program, so the qualifying scope and any retroactive lookback window vary by jurisdiction.

cpace-financing.q: Does my existing mortgage lender have to approve C-PACE?
cpace-financing.a: Most enabling statutes do not require senior lender consent, but nearly every first mortgage document restricts new assessments against the property. In practice the mortgage holder signs a consent or acknowledgment before the assessment records. Securing that acknowledgment early is the single most common cause of delay in a C-PACE closing.

cpace-financing.q: How much of a project can C-PACE fund?
cpace-financing.a: C-PACE usually covers 20% to 30% of total project cost and sits alongside, not in place of, senior debt and equity. Owners use it to lower the blended cost of capital, reduce the equity check, or fund improvements a construction lender will not advance against. Some programs also allow retroactive funding of recently completed work.

multifamily.q: What financing options are available for multifamily properties?
multifamily.a: Multifamily properties enjoy the broadest financing options in commercial real estate, including agency loans (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac), bank loans, life insurance company loans, CMBS, bridge loans, and construction financing. Agency programs offer the most competitive rates with non-recourse terms.

multifamily.q: What is the minimum size for a commercial multifamily loan?
multifamily.a: Most commercial multifamily loans apply to properties with 5 or more units, since 1-4 unit assets generally fall under residential lending guidelines. Commercial Lending Solutions handles multifamily financing requests starting at $2MM, with capital available for larger single assets and portfolios exceeding $100MM.

multifamily.q: What are current multifamily loan rates?
multifamily.a: Multifamily loan rates range from 5.34% to 8.25% depending on the lender type and deal specifics. Agency loans (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) offer the most competitive rates, typically 5.34% to 6.50% for stabilized properties with strong fundamentals.

multifamily.q: Can I finance manufactured housing communities?
multifamily.a: Yes. Manufactured housing communities (mobile home parks) qualify for competitive financing from agency lenders, banks, and life insurance companies. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac both have dedicated manufactured housing programs with favorable terms.

multifamily.q: What is the typical LTV for multifamily financing?
multifamily.a: Multifamily LTV ratios range from 65% to 80%, depending on the lender type. Agency programs can offer up to 80% LTV, while banks and life companies typically cap at 70-75%. Bridge loans for value-add multifamily may go up to 75-80% of as-is value.

multifamily.q: How do I qualify for agency multifamily financing?
multifamily.a: Agency financing (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) requires a stabilized property with minimum 90% occupancy, a debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.20x-1.25x minimum, a borrower with multifamily experience and strong net worth, and a property in good physical condition.

industrial.q: What are the best financing options for industrial properties?
industrial.a: Industrial properties qualify for competitive financing from banks, life insurance companies, CMBS lenders, and debt funds. Life companies offer the best rates for stabilized assets, while banks provide flexibility for portfolio deals. Bridge and construction loans are available for value-add and development.

industrial.q: What are current industrial loan rates?
industrial.a: Industrial loan rates range from 5.34% to 8.25% for permanent financing, with rates on the lower end for long-term credit-tenant net lease assets. Construction loans range from 6.79% to 10%+, and bridge loans fall in the 7-12% range depending on the transition strategy.

industrial.q: Can I finance cold storage and food processing facilities?
industrial.a: Yes. Cold storage and food processing facilities qualify for commercial financing, though they require lenders experienced with the specialized infrastructure and operating requirements. CLS CRE has closed over $87M in cold storage and food processing deals.

industrial.q: What is the typical LTV for industrial financing?
industrial.a: Industrial property LTV ratios range from 65% to 75% for permanent financing, with banks and life companies at the higher end for strong deals. Construction loans offer 65-80% of total project cost, and bridge loans provide 65-75% of as-is value.

industrial.q: Do industrial properties qualify for SBA loans?
industrial.a: Yes. Owner-occupied industrial properties (where the business occupies at least 51% of the space) qualify for SBA 504 and 7(a) loans with up to 90% financing. This is ideal for manufacturing, distribution, and production companies purchasing their own facilities.

industrial.q: How do lenders evaluate data center financing?
industrial.a: Data center financing is evaluated based on power infrastructure, connectivity, tenant quality, lease terms, and replacement cost. Lenders look for long-term leases with creditworthy tenants, redundant power and cooling systems, and strategic locations near fiber optic networks.

retail.a: Absolutely. While the retail sector has evolved, well-located properties with strong tenancy continue to attract competitive financing. Grocery-anchored centers, net lease properties with credit tenants, and experiential retail all remain highly financeable asset classes.

retail.q: What are the best financing sources for net lease retail?
retail.a: Single-tenant net lease retail with investment-grade tenants is highly attractive to life insurance companies and CMBS lenders, offering the most competitive long-term fixed rates. Banks also compete aggressively for net lease deals with strong tenancy.

retail.q: What are current retail property loan rates?
retail.a: Retail property loan rates range from 5.34% to 8.25% for permanent financing, with credit-tenant net lease assets at the lower end. Multi-tenant shopping centers may see rates at the higher end depending on tenancy strength and market location.

retail.q: Can I finance a restaurant with a commercial loan?
retail.a: Restaurants can be financed through SBA 504/7(a) programs if owner-occupied, or through conventional commercial loans if the property is leased to a restaurant operator. Stand-alone restaurant properties are considered higher risk and may require specialized lenders.

retail.q: What do lenders look for in retail property underwriting?
retail.a: Lenders evaluate tenant credit quality, lease terms and rollover schedule, in-place rent vs. market rent, anchor tenant presence, location and traffic counts, competitive landscape, and the property's physical condition and deferred maintenance.

office.q: Can I still get financing for office buildings?
office.a: Yes. While office lending has tightened since the pandemic, well-located office properties with strong tenancy, long-term leases, and low vacancy continue to attract financing from banks, life companies, and CMBS lenders. The key is demonstrating stable cash flow and tenant quality.

office.q: What are current office building loan rates?
office.a: Office building loan rates range from 5.75% to 8.50% for permanent financing, depending on property quality, tenancy, and market. Class A office in strong submarkets commands better terms than Class B/C in weaker markets.

office.q: What are the challenges of financing office in the current market?
office.a: Key challenges include remote work uncertainty, higher vacancy rates in many markets, tenant downsizing trends, and increased lender scrutiny of lease rollover risk. Properties with long-term leases to creditworthy tenants in strong submarkets remain financeable.

office.q: Can I get SBA financing for an owner-occupied office?
office.a: Yes. SBA 504 and 7(a) loans are excellent options for businesses purchasing their own office space. With up to 90% financing and below-market rates, SBA programs are ideal for professional service firms, medical practices, and other owner-occupiers.

office.q: How do lenders evaluate medical office properties?
office.a: Medical office is underwritten more favorably than general office due to higher tenant stickiness (practices invest heavily in buildout), longer lease terms, and recession-resistant demand. Lenders may offer higher LTV and lower rates for medical office compared to general office.

mixed-use.q: How do lenders underwrite mixed-use properties?
mixed-use.a: Lenders evaluate each component of a mixed-use property separately (residential, retail, office) and then blend the analysis. Properties with 80%+ residential may qualify for agency financing. The commercial component is underwritten based on in-place leases and market rent comparisons.

mixed-use.q: What are the financing challenges for mixed-use properties?
mixed-use.a: Mixed-use properties can be challenging because they straddle multiple underwriting frameworks. Lenders need to be comfortable with each use type, and the blended analysis may result in more conservative terms than a single-use property. Finding the right lender is key.

mixed-use.q: Can mixed-use properties qualify for agency financing?
mixed-use.a: Mixed-use properties with at least 80% residential use (by income or square footage) may qualify for Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac financing, benefiting from agency rates and non-recourse terms. The commercial component must comply with agency guidelines.

mixed-use.q: What are current mixed-use property loan rates?
mixed-use.a: Mixed-use property loan rates range from 5.50% to 8.50% depending on the lender, property composition, and market. Agency-eligible mixed-use (80%+ residential) can access rates in the 5.50% to 6.75% range.

mixed-use.q: Is construction financing available for mixed-use development?
mixed-use.a: Yes. Mixed-use construction loans are available from banks, debt funds, and private lenders. These projects typically require 20-35% borrower equity (65-80% loan-to-cost), strong development experience, and a clear permanent financing or sale exit strategy.

hospitality.q: How do lenders evaluate hotel financing?
hospitality.a: Hotel lenders evaluate revenue per available room (RevPAR), occupancy rates, average daily rate (ADR), brand affiliation, management quality, competitive set positioning, market supply/demand dynamics, and the property's physical condition and capital expenditure needs.

hospitality.q: What are current hotel financing rates?
hospitality.a: Hotel loan rates range from 6.00% to 9.00%+ for permanent financing, with flagged properties at the lower end and independent hotels at the higher end. Bridge and renovation loans range from 8.00% to 13.00% depending on the transition plan.

hospitality.q: Can I use SBA financing for a hotel?
hospitality.a: Yes. Owner-operated hotels qualify for SBA 504 and 7(a) financing with up to 85-90% leverage. This is ideal for smaller, independent hotels where the owner actively operates the business. Flagged hotels may also qualify if the owner meets SBA requirements.

hospitality.q: Is hospitality financing more expensive than other property types?
hospitality.a: Generally yes. Hotels are considered higher risk due to their operating business nature and revenue volatility. Rates are typically 50-200 basis points higher than comparable multifamily or industrial financing, and leverage may be more conservative.

hospitality.q: What is the minimum DSCR for hotel financing?
hospitality.a: Most hotel lenders require a minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.35x to 1.50x, compared to 1.20x to 1.25x for stabilized multifamily or industrial properties. Higher DSCR requirements reflect the operating business risk inherent in hospitality assets.

self-storage.q: What financing options are available for self-storage facilities?
self-storage.a: Self-storage facilities qualify for bank permanent loans, life insurance company loans, CMBS financing, bridge loans, construction loans, SBA 504 (owner-operated), and specialty self-storage lenders. Stabilized facilities with 85%+ occupancy and professional management attract the most competitive terms.

self-storage.q: What are current self-storage loan rates?
self-storage.a: Self-storage permanent loan rates typically range from 5.50% to 7.50% depending on lender type, facility quality, occupancy, and market. Climate-controlled, institutional-quality facilities in strong markets receive the best rates. Bridge and construction loans range from 7.00% to 11.00%.

self-storage.q: What do lenders look for in self-storage financing?
self-storage.a: Lenders evaluate physical occupancy (typically requiring 80%+ for permanent financing), economic occupancy, revenue per square foot, market supply/demand dynamics, facility condition, climate control features, security systems, and management quality. Facilities with strong net operating income trends and diverse tenant bases are most attractive.

self-storage.q: Can I finance a self-storage conversion project?
self-storage.a: Yes. Converting big-box retail, industrial, or office buildings into self-storage is a growing strategy. Bridge lenders and construction lenders finance conversions, typically requiring 60-75% of total project cost. The key underwriting factor is demonstrating unmet storage demand in the trade area.

self-storage.q: What is the typical LTV for self-storage loans?
self-storage.a: Permanent self-storage loans typically offer 65-75% LTV from banks and life companies, up to 75% from CMBS lenders. SBA 504 financing can reach 85-90% LTV for owner-operators. Bridge loans for value-add or lease-up situations typically max at 70-80% of as-is value.

data-centers.q: How is data center financing different from industrial financing?
data-centers.a: Data center financing is significantly more specialized than conventional industrial lending. Lenders evaluate power capacity (megawatts), redundancy levels (Tier classification), cooling infrastructure, connectivity and fiber access, tenant credit quality, and the cost of power in the local market. The capital-intensive nature of data centers and specialized build-out requirements mean higher per-square-foot values and different underwriting metrics than standard warehouse or distribution space.

data-centers.q: What are current data center loan rates?
data-centers.a: Data center permanent loan rates range from 5.25% to 7.25% for stabilized, leased facilities with creditworthy tenants. Single-tenant data centers leased to hyperscalers or investment-grade enterprises receive the most competitive rates. Bridge and development financing ranges from 7.00% to 10.00%+ depending on the lease status and tenant profile.

data-centers.q: What is the minimum loan size for data center financing?
data-centers.a: Due to the capital-intensive nature of data centers, most lenders set higher minimums than conventional CRE. Bank and life company permanent loans typically start at $5M-$10M, while CMBS and institutional lenders often require $10M+ loan amounts. Edge and smaller colocation facilities may access financing starting at $2M-$5M from regional banks.

data-centers.q: Can I finance a data center development project?
data-centers.a: Yes. Ground-up data center construction financing is available from banks, debt funds, and specialty infrastructure lenders. Lenders typically require pre-leasing commitments from creditworthy tenants, experienced development sponsorship, and demonstrated power availability. Construction loans cover 60-70% of total project cost with interest reserves for the build and lease-up period.

data-centers.q: What makes a data center investment attractive to lenders?
data-centers.a: Lenders favor data centers with long-term leases (10-20 years) to credit-rated tenants, adequate power infrastructure with utility commitments, Tier III or IV redundancy, diverse fiber connectivity, and location in established data center markets with favorable power costs. The essential nature of digital infrastructure and high switching costs for tenants provide strong downside protection.

senior-living.q: What financing programs are available for senior living facilities?
senior-living.a: Senior living facilities can access HUD/FHA 232 loans (the most competitive permanent option), bank permanent loans, bridge loans, CMBS financing, construction loans, mezzanine capital, and SBA 504 for owner-operated facilities. The best financing option depends on the facility type (IL, AL, MC, SNF), stabilization status, and operator track record.

senior-living.q: What is HUD 232 financing for senior living?
senior-living.a: HUD 232 is a government-insured mortgage program specifically for residential care facilities including assisted living, nursing homes, and board and care homes. It offers the most aggressive terms in senior housing: up to 85% LTV for refinances, 40-year fully amortizing terms, non-recourse, and some of the lowest fixed rates available. The trade-off is a longer closing timeline (4-6 months) and significant regulatory requirements.

senior-living.q: How do lenders underwrite assisted living facilities?
senior-living.a: Assisted living lenders evaluate occupancy rates, revenue per occupied unit, staffing ratios and labor costs, regulatory compliance history, state licensing status, operator experience, resident acuity mix, local demographic trends (75+ population growth), and competitive supply in the trade area. Strong operators with proven track records and facilities in markets with favorable demographics receive the best terms.

senior-living.q: Is senior living financing more expensive than multifamily?
senior-living.a: Yes, generally 50-150 basis points higher than conventional multifamily due to the operating business component and regulatory complexity. However, HUD 232 permanent financing offers rates comparable to agency multifamily. The higher cost reflects the healthcare operational risk, state licensing requirements, and the more intensive management needed for senior care facilities.

senior-living.q: What occupancy rate do lenders require for senior living?
senior-living.a: Most permanent lenders require 85-90%+ stabilized occupancy for senior living facilities, though this varies by care type. Independent living may qualify at 85%, while assisted living and memory care typically need 88-90%+ to demonstrate stabilization. Bridge lenders will finance facilities at 60-80% occupancy for lease-up or turnaround situations.

medical-office.q: Why do lenders favor medical office buildings?
medical-office.a: Lenders favor medical office buildings because healthcare is a non-discretionary service, making tenant demand recession-resistant. Medical tenants sign longer leases (7-15 years vs. 3-5 for general office) due to expensive specialized build-outs, creating stable long-term cash flows. Creditworthy health system tenants and the aging population driving healthcare demand further strengthen the lending thesis.

medical-office.q: What are current medical office loan rates?
medical-office.a: Medical office permanent loan rates typically range from 5.25% to 7.00%, which is generally 25-50 basis points lower than comparable general office properties due to the stronger fundamentals. Life insurance companies and CMBS lenders offer the most competitive rates for stabilized MOBs with long-term health system leases. Bridge and construction loans range from 7.00% to 10.00%.

medical-office.q: Does the location of a medical office building affect financing?
medical-office.a: Yes, significantly. On-campus or adjacent-to-hospital medical office buildings receive the most favorable financing terms because of the built-in patient referral network and tenant stability. Off-campus MOBs in healthcare corridors or near major medical centers also finance well. Standalone medical offices in suburban locations may face slightly higher rates and lower LTV limits.

medical-office.q: Can I use SBA financing for a medical office?
medical-office.a: Yes. Owner-occupied medical office buildings qualify for SBA 504 and 7(a) financing with as little as 10% down. This is ideal for physician groups, dental practices, veterinary hospitals, and specialty clinics purchasing their own building. SBA financing offers below-market fixed rates and 25-year amortization.

medical-office.q: What is the typical lease structure for medical office tenants?
medical-office.a: Medical office leases are typically NNN (triple net) or modified gross, with 7-15 year initial terms and multiple renewal options. Tenant improvement allowances are higher than general office due to specialized build-outs (plumbing, electrical, lead-lined walls for imaging). Lenders view these long leases and high switching costs favorably, often offering higher LTV and lower rates than general office.
